msg:
All Trello issues are linked to Github issues. Yellow means it’s in-progress. Green means it’s completed. Github issues have a checklist of items to complete. Here’s how I think you could use the system effectively:1. Start using branches for the mobile repos. Name each branch after a Github issue. Put all commits related to that issue in that branch. Complete the Github issue checklist as you make progress on the issue/branch.

2. When the branch is ready, make a pull request. So, for example, if it’s Android, then you or @fxpage will make the PR. Have each other review it and merge to master it if it looks good.

3. When you make the PR, be sure to reference the Github issue you’re working on. This will automatically close the issue when the PR is merged.

4. When I see that a PR is merged, I’ll take care of updating the relevant Trello card from Yellow to Green so that both your team and myself are aware of the progress. So, Trello will act as our ultimate progress indicator. (edited)

9:13 Going forward, we’ll keep the same issues in Github and cards in Trello — these represents parts of our application. We will simply close/open the issues and change the cards from yellow to green as necessary. We’ll update the specific checklist in each Github issue for each new sprint. This will give us a good overview of what parts of the app are being worked on, and which aren’t.

The management of the business aspects of healthcare organizations, such as aging services providers, allied health facilities, hospitals, surgical centers, and physician group practices is health administration

Health systems management ensures that specific outcomes are attained, that departments within a health facility are running smoothly, that the right people are in the right jobs, that people know what is expected of them, that resources are used efficiently and that all departments are working towards a common goal.

Hospital administrators are individuals or groups of people who act as the central point of control within hospitals. These individuals may be previous or current clinicians, or individuals with other backgrounds. There are two types of administrators, generalists and specialists. Generalists are individuals who are responsible for managing or helping to manage an entire facility. Specialists are individuals who are responsible for the efficient operations of a specific department such as policy analysis, finance, accounting, budgeting, human resources, or marketing.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) classified emergency departments into two types: Type A, the majority, which are open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year; and those who are not, Type B. Many US emergency departments are exceedingly busy. A study found that in 2009, there were an estimated 128,885,040 ED encounters in US hospitals. Approximately one-fifth of ED visits in 2010 were for patients under the age of 18 years.[7] In 2009–2010, a total of 19.6 million emergency department visits in the United States were made by persons aged 65 and over.[8] Most encounters (82.8 percent) resulted in treatment and release; 17.2 percent were admitted to inpatient care.

Hospital administration is one the largest industries in the U.S. and is the most popular subfield of health administration and management. Hospital administrators are vital to ensuring that medical facilities run efficiently and deliver quality care. They manage the the business operations and are typically responsible for staffing, budgets, public relations, patient rights, finances, and other administrative tasks.

Hospital administrators enjoy rewarding, challenging, and often high-paying positions in which they fill a broad range of leadership roles. A strong job market outlook across a wide range of industries, such as nursing care facilities, offices of physicians, and outpatient care centers, have led to an increase in need for qualified personnel.

In my daily work as a primary care internist, I see no letup from pain. Every single patient, it seems, has an aching shoulder or a bum knee or a painful back. “Our bodies evolved to live about 40 years,” I always explain, “and then be finished off by a mammoth or a microbe.” Thanks to a century of staggering medical progress, we now live past 80, but evolution hasn’t caught up; the cartilage in our joints still wears down in our 40s, and we are more obese and more sedentary than we used to be, which doesn’t help.

So it’s no surprise that chronic arthritis and back pain are the second and third most common non-acute reasons that people go to the doctor and that pain costs America up to $635 billion annually. The pain remedies developed by the pharmaceutical industry are only modestly effective, and they have side effects that range from nausea and constipation to addiction and death.

In 2014, researchers in Canada did an interesting study about the role of communication in the treatment of chronic back pain. Half the patients in the study received mild electrical stimulation from physical therapists, and half received sham stimulation (all the equipment is set up, but the electrical current is never activated).
